Left: talent and luck both point to success and are not joined to each other, an unshielded collider, drawn in the accent color. Right: x and y both point to z, but the edge x to y, left in full ink, links the two causes, so this collider is shielded and faded. The card returns the only v-structure, (talent, success, luck), and notes that (x, z, y) is shielded by x to y." width="100%"} A v-structure (an *unshielded* collider) is a triple `p1 -> c <- p2` where `p1` and `p2` are not joined by an edge. V-structures are what distinguishes Markov-equivalent causal DAGs: two DAGs encode the same conditional independences exactly when they share their skeleton and their v-structures (Verma and Pearl, 1990), so causal discovery algorithms such as PC orient edges by finding them. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Every v-structure `(p1, c, p2)` as node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Filters `colliders()` for parent pairs with no edge in either direction. Matches NetworkX's `dag.v_structures`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Talent and luck both cause success, but A -> B -> C is a chain, not a v-structure, and a collider whose causes are linked is "shielded": ::: {#59cbf0ce .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["talent", "luck", "success", "x", "y", "z"]) g.add_edges([("talent", "success"), ("luck", "success"), ("x", "z"), ("y", "z"), ("x", "y")]) [tuple(g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in t) for t in g.v_structures()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [('talent', 'success', 'luck')] ``` ::: :::
